rail_guard.text: Keswick Station. The old line closed in 1972, but the Wildlore rail has the good sense to keep the platform. Trains for every station you have visited. Mind the gap, the sheep and the weather.

sheep_herdwick.text: A Herdwick, up on the hill. It has been here for a thousand years, give or take a lamb.

kes_boatman.text: The launches go round the lake every hour, stopping at jetties for walkers. We're the buses of Derwentwater, and the passengers are usually damp.
The lake has a floating island. In hot summers a mat of weed rises from the bottom, and it can carry a dog. Please don't test that.

kes_pencil.text: A pencil isn't lead, of course. It's graphite, and there's a very good story about how a storm in Borrowdale found it in the 1500s, when the roots of a fallen tree exposed the seam.
For years, graphite was so valuable that guards watched the mine. It was used for casting cannonballs, and for the very first pencils. I'm told the cannonballs are less common now.

kes_walker.text: Catbells, Skiddaw, Latrigg. All walkable from here, and all with a view of Derwentwater. I'm doing the three before lunch. I mean the three before tea.
Keswick has more outdoor shops than anywhere I've ever seen. They're all slightly different shades of green.

kes_hotelier.text: Welcome! Breakfast is at eight, which includes black pudding, because it's the Lakes. The washing line is for socks. If the weather is dry, which it's not, you may use it.
We get four hundred days of rain a year here. I'm told that's mathematically impossible. Come and tell the clouds.

kes_ice.text: Rum and raisin, or Kendal mint cake in cone form. Kendal mint cake has been taken up Everest. It was in the pocket of a man who got to the top. I'm not saying it's the reason.
Cumberland sausage: a coil, never a link. Cumberland people are very particular. Ask them.
